title: Quiet Cracking and Its Impact on Mental Health
summary: Quiet cracking is a quiet erosion of well-being at work and home. A therapist explains what quiet cracking is, its signs, and how to get help.
body_markdown:
## Quiet Cracking in Parenting


Although quiet cracking started as a workplace term, the same slow erosion is increasingly recognized in parents, who carry a relentless, around-the-clock load that rarely lets up. The mechanics are nearly identical: persistent demands that outpace available resources, a feeling of being unseen, and the expectation to keep functioning no matter what. Reporting from[Parents.com on quiet cracking](https://www.parents.com/more-parents-are-quiet-cracking-heres-how-to-make-the-stress-more-bearable-11989278#toc-building-community-part-of-the-antidote) in parenting describes mothers and fathers running on empty while still managing every school pickup, meal, and bedtime.


One important distinction is worth drawing here. A related workplace concept, quiet quitting, describes deliberately doing the bare minimum and mentally checking out of a job. That framing can make sense at work, where someone can choose to disengage from tasks beyond their pay. It does not translate to parenting. A caregiver cannot quietly quit a child, and the demands do not pause; this is part of why the parental version of cracking can be so isolating.


A 2024 systematic review in BMC Public Health found that parental burnout, a chronic stress syndrome born from prolonged caregiving demands, is associated with anxiety and depressive symptoms and can affect any parent regardless of background. Mothers often shoulder a disproportionate share of this load, which is reflected in broader trends in[maternal mental health](https://lifestance.com/blog/maternal-mental-health-decline-statistics-insights/) . Recognizing the cracks early, in yourself or a co-parent, is the first step toward keeping ordinary parenting stress from hardening into something more serious.
